source_text: Τὴν γὰρ στερρότητα καὶ ἀντιτυπίαν τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ ἐναπολαμβανομένου ταῖς κοιλότησι τῶν νεφῶν, καὶ διὰ τὸ βιαίως ἐκρήγνυσθαι τοὺς κατὰ τὰς βροντὰς ἀποτελοῦντος ψόφους, στερέωσιν βροντῆς ἡ Γραφὴ προσηγόρευσεν. Καὶ νῦν τοίνυν ἡγούμεθα ἐπί τινος στερρᾶς φύσεως, στέγειν τοῦ ὕδατος τὸ ὀλισθηρὸν καὶ εὐδιάλυτον ἐξαρκούσης, τὴν φωνὴν ταύτην τετάχθαι. Καὶ οὐ δήπου, ἐπειδὴ κατὰ τὴν κοινὴν ἐκδοχὴν ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος δοκεῖ τὴν γένεσιν ἐσχηκέναι, ἢ ὕδατι πεπηγότι ἐμφερὲς εἶναι προσήκει νομίζειν, ἤ τινι τοιαύτῃ ὕλῃ ἐκ τῆς τοῦ ὑγροῦ διηθήσεως τὴν ἀρχὴν λαμβανούσῃ, ὁποία ἐστὶν ἥ τε τοῦ κρυστάλλου λίθου, ὃν δι' ὑπερβάλλουσαν τοῦ ὕδατος πῆξιν μεταποιεῖσθαί φασιν, ἢ ἡ τοῦ σπέκλου φύσις ἐν μετάλλοις συνισταμένη. Λίθος δέ ἐστι διαυγὴς, ἰδιάζουσαν καὶ καθαρωτάτην τὴν διαφάνειαν κεκτημένος, ὃς ἐὰν κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φύσιν ἀκριβὴς εὑρεθῇ, μήτε κατεδηδεσμένος σηπεδόνι τινὶ, μήτε τὸ βάθος ὑπερρηγμένος ταῖς διαφύσεσι, μικροῦ τῷ ἀέρι τὴν διαύγειαν ἔοικεν. Οὐδενὶ οὖν τούτων εἰκάζομεν τὸ στερέωμα. Παιδικῆς γὰρ τῷ ὄντι καὶ ἁπλῆς διανοίας, τοιαύτας ἔχειν περὶ τῶν οὐρανίων τὰς ὑπολήψεις. Οὐ μὴν, οὐδὲ εἰ πάντα ἐν ἅπασίν ἐστι, πῦρ μὲν ἐν γῇ, ἀὴρ δὲ ἐν ὕδατι, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὡσαύτως ἐν ἑτέρῳ τὸ ἕτερον· καὶ μηδὲν τῶν αἰσθήσει ὑποπιπτόντων στοιχείων εἰλικρινές ἐστι καὶ ἀμιγὲς, ἢ τῆς πρὸς τὸ μέσον, ἢ τῆς πρὸς τὸ ἀντι κείμενον κοινωνίας· τούτου ἕνεκεν καταδεχόμεθα, τὸ στερέωμα ἢ ἐξ ἑνὸς τῶν ἁπλῶν, ἢ τὸ ἀπὸ τούτων μίγμα φῆσαι ὑπάρχειν, δεδιδαγμένοι παρὰ τῆς Γραφῆς, μηδὲν ἐπιτρέπειν ἡμῶν τῷ νῷ πέρα τῶν συγκεχωρημένων φαντασιοῦσθαι. Μὴ παραδράμῃ δὲ ἡμᾶς μηδὲ ἐκεῖνο ἀπαρασήμαντον, ὅτι μετὰ τὸ προστάξαι τὸν Θεὸν, Γενηθήτω στερέωμα, οὐκ εἴρηται ἁπλῶς, καὶ ἐγένετο στερέωμα· ἀλλὰ, Καὶ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ στερέωμα· καὶ πάλιν, Διεχώρισεν ὁ Θεός. Οἱ κωφοὶ ἀκούσατε, καὶ οἱ τυφλοὶ ἀναβλέψατε. Καὶ τίς κωφὸς, ἀλλ' ἢ ὁ μὴ ἀκούων οὕτω μεγαλοφώνως ἐμβοῶντος τοῦ Πνεύματος; Καὶ τίς τυφλός; Ὁ μὴ ἐνορῶν ταῖς οὕτως ἐναργέσι περὶ τοῦ Μονογενοῦς ἀποδείξεσι. Γενηθήτω στερέωμα. Αὕτη ἡ φωνὴ τῆς προκαταρκτικῆς αἰτίας. Ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ στερέωμα. Αὕτη τῆς ποιητικῆς καὶ δημιουργικῆς δυνάμεως μαρτυρία. 3.5 Ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τὰ συνεχῆ τῆς ἐξηγήσεως τὸν λόγον ἐπανα γάγωμεν. Ἔστω διαχωρίζον, φησὶν, ἀνὰ μέσον ὕδατος καὶ ὕδατος. Ἄπειρος μὲν ἦν, ὡς ἔοικε, τῶν ὑδάτων ἡ χύσις, πανταχόθεν ἐπικυμαινόντων τῇ γῇ καὶ ἀπαιωρουμένων αὐτῆς· ὡς καὶ τὴν πρὸς τὰ ἄλλα στοιχεῖα δοκεῖν ἀναλογίαν ἐκβαίνειν. Διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ ἐν τοῖς κατόπιν ἐλέγετο ἄβυσσος πανταχόθεν περιβεβλῆσθαι τῇ γῇ. Τὴν δὲ αἰτίαν τοῦ πλήθους ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς ἀποδώσομεν. Πάντως δὲ οὐδεὶς ὑμῶν οὐδὲ τῶν πάνυ κατησκημένων τὸν νοῦν, καὶ περὶ τὴν φθειρομένην ταύτην καὶ ῥέουσαν φύσιν ὀξυωπούντων, ἐπισκήψει τῇ δόξῃ, ὡς ἀδύνατα ἢ πλασματώδη ὑποτιθεμένων κατὰ τὸν λόγον· οὐδὲ ἀπαιτήσει ἡμᾶς εὐθύνας, ἐπὶ τίνος ἡ τῶν ὑδάτων ἥδραστο φύσις. Ὧ γὰρ λόγῳ τὴν γῆν βαρυτέραν οὖσαν τοῦ ὕδατος ἀπαιωροῦσι τοῦ μέσου τῶν ἐσχάτων ἀπάγοντες, τῷ αὐτῷ δήπου πάντως καὶ τὸ μυρίον ὕδωρ ἐκεῖνο, διά τε τὴν κατὰ φύσιν ἐπὶ τὸ κάτω φορὰν, καὶ διὰ τὴν πανταχόθεν ἰσορροπίαν, περὶ τὴν γῆν ἀτρεμεῖν συγχωρήσουσιν.
thought_title: The firmament is solid but not ice or crystal
orientation: Basil is explaining the firmament God commands on the second day to divide water from water.
pass_a_gloss: For the solidity and resistance of the wind that is caught in the hollows of the clouds, and that produces the sounds at the thunders through bursting out violently, Scripture called making firm of thunder. And now therefore we hold that this utterance has been appointed with reference to some solid nature, which is sufficient to hold back the slippery and easily dissolved character of the water. And surely it is not right, because according to the common understanding it seems to have had its origin from water, to think that it is like water that has congealed, or like some such matter that takes its beginning from filtering of liquid, such as is both the stone of crystal, which they say is transformed through excessive congealing of water, and the nature of mica that forms in mines. And it is a transparent stone, possessing a peculiar and purest transparency, which if it is found exact according to its own nature, neither bound down by any decay nor broken across in its depth by cleavages, almost resembles air in clearness. To none of these things therefore do we liken the firmament. For it belongs in truth to a childish and simple mind to hold such suppositions about heavenly things. But neither, even if all things are in all, fire in earth and air in water, and likewise of the rest one thing in another, and none of the elements that fall under sense is pure and unmixed, either with respect to sharing toward the middle or with respect to sharing toward the opposite, for this reason do we accept to say that the firmament exists either from one of the simple elements or as the mixture from these, since we have been taught by Scripture to allow our mind to imagine nothing beyond what has been conceded. But let not even that pass by us unmarked, that after God commanded, Let there be a firmament, it was not said simply, and there was a firmament, but, And God made the firmament, and again, God divided. Deaf ones, hear, and blind ones, look up. And who is deaf, except the one who does not hear the Spirit crying out so loudly? And who is blind? The one who does not see proofs about the only Son so clear. Let there be a firmament. This is the voice of the preliminary cause. God made the firmament. This is testimony of the making and fashioning power. But let us bring our account back to the continuations of the exposition. Let it be dividing, he says, in the middle of water and water. Boundless was, as it seems, the pouring of the waters, surging over the earth from everywhere and hanging above it, so as even to seem to go beyond the proportion toward the other elements. For on this account in the preceding words it was said that the deep had been thrown around the earth from everywhere. And the cause of the multitude we shall give in what follows. In any case no one of you, not even those thoroughly trained in mind and keen in sight concerning this corruptible and flowing nature, will find fault with the opinion, as if we suppose impossible or invented things in our account, nor will demand from us a reckoning, on what the nature of the waters was fastened. For by whatever reasoning they suspend the earth, although it is heavier than water, in the middle while drawing it away from the outermost bounds, by this same reasoning surely they will also allow that that countless water remains still around the earth, both through its natural rush toward below and through its balance from everywhere.

choices.why: στερέωσις is the act of making firm, parallel to making firm the wind caught in clouds, not the created firmament

choices.english: we hold that this utterance has been appointed
choices.why: ἡγούμεθα is an opinion verb and τετάχθαι is perfect passive infinitive of appointment, keeping who judges and what was done
rejected: we are led to a solid nature

choices.why: προκαταρκτική distinguishes the commanding voice Let there be from the executive making, as first cause versus effecting power
both adjectives describe productive divine efficacy attested by God made, not human artistry

choices.english: drawing it away from the outermost bounds
choices.why: ἀπάγοντες is active participle of leading away, so the earth is held in the middle by being drawn away from extremes

pass_b_english: Scripture speaks of the solidity and resistance of the wind that is caught in the hollows of the clouds. When that wind bursts out violently, it produces the sounds of thunder. Scripture called this force the making firm of thunder (Amos 4:13). Basil says we hold that this utterance about the firmament has been appointed for a different purpose: for a solid nature strong enough to hold back what is slippery and easily dissolved in water.

That does not mean we should suppose the firmament looks like frozen water, merely because the common view holds that it takes its origin from water. Nor should we suppose it is made of some matter that begins when moisture is filtered, like crystal stone or like the mica that forms in mines. People say water is changed into crystal stone by extreme freezing. Mica is a transparent stone with its own very pure clearness. If a piece is found true to its nature, neither eaten away by any decay nor split through its depth by cracks, its brightness is almost like air. Basil says we liken the firmament to none of these things. To hold such notions about heaven is truly the mark of a childish and simple mind. It is true that all things are in all things: fire is in earth, air is in water, and each of the other elements is likewise in another. None of the elements perceived by the senses is pure and unmixed, whether by sharing in what tends toward the middle or in what tends toward its opposite. For that reason Basil says we do not accept saying that the firmament either comes from one of the simple elements or is a mixture made from them. Scripture has taught us to allow our minds to imagine nothing beyond what has been granted.

Basil says we should not pass over one point without marking it. After God gave the command, “Let there be a firmament” (Genesis 1:6), Scripture does not simply add, “and there was a firmament.” It says instead, “And God made the firmament” (Genesis 1:7), and again, “God divided.” Scripture says, “You deaf, hear, and you blind, look up” (Isaiah 42:18). Basil asks who is deaf except the one who does not hear the Spirit crying out so loudly. And who is blind except the one who does not see such clear proofs concerning the only Son. “Let there be a firmament” is the voice of the preliminary cause. “God made the firmament” bears witness to his making and fashioning power.

But Basil says let us return our speech to the course of the explanation. God says, “Let it be dividing between water and water” (Genesis 1:6). The outpouring of the waters was boundless, it seems, surging over the earth from every side and hanging above it, so that it seemed to exceed its due proportion to the other elements. For this reason it was said earlier that the earth was clothed all around by the deep. Basil says he will give the reason for this abundance later. Certainly none of you will object to this account as if it assumed impossible or invented things, not even those among you whose minds are highly trained and keenly observant of this perishable and fleeting nature. Nor will you demand from us an account of what the nature of the waters rested upon. By the same reasoning by which they hold the earth suspended in the middle, though it is heavier than water, drawing it away from the outermost bounds, they will surely also grant that the countless water rests motionless around the earth, both because it naturally moves downward and because it is evenly balanced on every side.
notes: spacing splits in source read as single words: ἀντι κείμενον as ἀντικείμενον, ἐπανα γάγωμεν as ἐπαναγάγωμεν; gloss follows normal sense, no text invented

problems.why: The phrase 'strengthening/establishing thunder' is from Amos 4:13 (LXX). Job 37:4 does not say it.

problems.quote: People say crystal is changed into stone by the extreme freezing of water.
problems.source_quote: ὃν δι' ὑπερβάλλουσαν τοῦ ὕδατος πῆξιν μεταποιεῖσθαί φασιν
problems.why: Reverses direction: water freezes into crystal, not crystal into stone.
problems.fix: People say water is turned into crystal stone by extreme freezing.
problems.ruling: ὃν δι' ὑπερβάλλουσαν τοῦ ὕδατος πῆξιν μεταποιεῖσθαί φασιν: ὃν = crystal, said to be changed (from water) by excess freezing. English says crystal becomes stone, misleading.

edits.old: People say crystal is changed into stone by the extreme freezing of water.
edits.new: People say water is changed into crystal stone by extreme freezing.

fixed: wrong_scripture: fixed — source has στερέωσιν βροντῆς, which is Amos 4:13 (στερεῶν βροντὴν), not Job 37:4.
mistranslation: fixed — source ὃν...μεταποιεῖσθαί φασιν means water is transformed into crystal stone, not crystal into stone.

last_rejected.quote: It is true that all things are in all things
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐ μὴν, οὐδὲ εἰ πάντα ἐν ἅπασίν ἐστι
last_rejected.why: The source is concessive and negated: not even if all things are in all things do we accept this. The English turns it into an affirmed premise with 'For that reason', which reverses the logic.
last_rejected.fix: Nor, even if all things are in all things (fire in earth, air in water) and no element is pure, do we accept saying the firmament is one of the simple elements or a mixture of them.
last_rejected.ruling: English keeps 'we do not accept' matching 'Οὐ...καταδεχόμεθα'; 'τούτου ἕνεκεν' preserved; concessive 'οὐδὲ εἰ' to assertive is nuance, conclusion unchanged.

last_rejected.quote: has been appointed for a different purpose: for a solid nature
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐπί τινος στερρᾶς φύσεως, στέγειν τοῦ ὕδατος τὸ ὀλισθηρὸν καὶ εὐδιάλυτον ἐξαρκούσης, τὴν φωνὴν ταύτην τετάχθαι
last_rejected.why: The source says the word 'firmament' is applied to a solid nature able to hold back water. 'A different purpose' is not in the source and implies a contrast it does not make.
last_rejected.fix: we hold that this word has been applied to a solid nature strong enough to hold back what is slippery and easily dissolved in water.
last_rejected.ruling: No 'different' in 'ἐπί τινος στερρᾶς φύσεως...τετάχθαι'; but 'Καὶ νῦν' signals new use, gloss harmless, solid-nature meaning intact.
